articles.title: Indian solar mission's new findings throw light on enduring Sun mysteries
articles.description:
By

Geeta Pandey

BBC Correspondent

,

Reporting from

Delhi

Published

34 minutes ago

One of the most enduring mysteries that has been puzzling scientists forever is how the Sun's outer atmosphere - the corona - is millions of degrees hotter than its surface. And how does the corona continue to remain so hot despite frequent eruptions during which it loses huge amounts of energy?

Astrophysicists in India now say the latest findings from

Aditya-L1

, the country's first solar observation mission in space, have provided them some vital clues to unlocking those mysteries. Their findings are revealed in a recent paper published in the prestigious Astrophysical Journal Letters.

The temperature variations in different regions of the Sun defy the laws of physics, says leading Indian solar astrophysicist Prof R Ramesh of the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA) who led the study.

If you cut through the Sun's layers, deep inside is the core where the temperature is 15 million Celsius. Travel outwards to the surface or the photosphere - the part that we see from the Earth - it's about 5,500C. Far away from the core is the Sun's outermost layer or corona where the temperature is about 2 million C - it can sometimes go up to 40 million C.

Prof Ramesh says the corona is where extreme weather events - such as solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs) - originate, during which large amounts of energy is released by the Sun into space. The CMEs cause beautiful auroras, and they can also affect life on Earth by causing geomagnetic storms that can knock down power grids and affect weather and communication satellites.

In normal or low-activity times, the Sun launches two to three CMEs a day. During the maximum solar activity cycle that comes every 11 years, there can be 10 or more in a single day.

"Now if the Sun is losing such huge amounts of energy with each CME and it's not replenished, the star at the centre of our solar system would lose all its energy and Earth would plunge into an irreversible deep freeze," Prof Ramesh says.

But since that's not happening, it means there's a "mechanism" by which the corona is able to maintain its inexplicably high temperature, he says.

Scientists put it down to two factors - one, the bubbling boiling motions on the Sun's surface that constantly generate waves which, as they travel outwards, carry energy to the corona - a bit like sea waves carrying foam and froth to the shore.

The second is the "tangled magnetic field lines" in the Sun's atmosphere that constantly snap and then reconnect. Prof Ramesh says a CME occurs when these twisting, looping lines - which resemble braided hair - rupture, throwing out massive clouds of magnetised plasma and gas in space. They often originate near sunspots, which are darker, cooler spots on the Sun where magnetic fields are particularly strong.

"But then these lines reconnect and the Sun replenishes the lost energy back within hours," he adds.

Why 2026 will be a year like no other for India's Sun mission

How important are India's Moon mission findings?

Why it costs India so little to reach the Moon and Mars

In their paper, Prof Ramesh says they have been able to quantify how much energy each of the two systems supply to the corona – which explains both why it's so many times hotter to begin with and how it retains that temperature after consistently losing energy.

Their study, he says, clearly shows that it's the second system that supplies most of the energy.

"Though the waves generated as a result of the bubbling, boiling motions on the Sun's surface generate and transport energy, their contribution is very little - they supply only 7% of the energy requirement.

"The remaining 93% comes because the Sun reconfigures itself and replenishes the lost energy."

To arrive at that calculation, Prof Ramesh says they studied a "very energetic" CME that took place on 5 August 2024. Emissions were recorded by Aditya-L1's coronagraph called Velc (Visible Emission Line Coronagraph).

"We saw that in 10 hours after the CME, the tangled field lines were able to go back to their original place, they reconnected and corona's energy was reconfigured," he said.

Aditya-L1: India's Sun mission reaches final destination

Chandrayaan-3: India makes historic landing near Moon's south pole

"We do recognise that energy generated by bubbly motions plays a major role in it, but we have evidence that it is not sufficient. Our study shows that the magnetic field lines snapping and reconnecting everywhere on the Sun are the primary source for supplying most of the energy."

These data, Prof Ramesh says, "provide an important benchmark" for future studies into the potential energy generation mechanisms in the Sun's atmosphere.

"I think they would help answer the fundamental questions of physics that defy logic," he says.

articles.title: You got hold of eclipse glasses just in time - here's what to do with them now
articles.description:
By

George Sandeman

Published

1 hour ago

Millions of us were treated to a stunning spectacle on Wednesday during mainland Europe's first total solar eclipse for more than 25 years.

And for some in the UK, it was a race against time to find a pair of eye-protecting eclipse glasses as shortages grew.

If you did manage to grab some, you might be asking - what do I do with them now?

"Eclipse glasses are a great example of our single-use culture," says Dr Renee Tonkin, the founder of Science Owl, an environmental education organisation focused on waste.

"Particularly because they're difficult to recycle due to their mixed materials."

According to Recycle Now, which advises on appropriate places to recycle items, the glasses are not wholly recyclable in your household waste.

It says you can recycle the cardboard frames so long as you separate them from the lenses, which are harder to recycle.

So here are three things you can do with those retina-saving spectacles.

Eclipse warning: The key signs you may have damaged your eyes

Published

12 hours ago

Millions watch 'surreal' solar eclipse in UK and Europe

Published

1 day ago

Save them for the 'eclipse of the century'

In 2027, parts of the world will be treated to a total solar eclipse - described by some as the "eclipse of the century" because of how long it will be visible for.

A

total solar eclipse

means the Moon's disk will completely cover the Sun - and it is expected to last for six minutes and 23 seconds, the longest on land since 1991.

We won't see a longer solar eclipse from land until 2114.

So, you might consider keeping your eclipse glasses to protect your eyes if you're planning a trip to watch next year's spectacle.

It takes place on 2 August 2027 and will be visible from southern Spain, in cities such as Malaga, as well as northern Africa and the Arabian peninsula.

Viewing in northern Africa is likely to be particularly good as few clouds are in the sky at that time of year.

The length of the totality on land will make next year's eclipse remarkable, says Dr Ed Bloomer, an astronomer at the Royal Observatory Greenwich.

"However, it's not going to be the eclipse of our century for us here in the UK because it's not going to trouble us at all," he added.

That said, he points out there will be more eclipses in the UK over the coming years - including the next partial solar eclipse in January 2028 - so you can always keep your glasses until then.

"The glasses that you get now - ones that are made to the correct

ISO [safety certification] standard

,

external

- are made slightly differently than older glasses," he says. "So you can keep them for longer periods."

Though he says you must keep them in a safe place to ensure the coating on the lenses isn't torn, worn or damaged, as that would make them unsafe to use again.

Donate them to others

If you can't travel to see next year's spectacle or don't want to keep your solar glasses for future partial eclipses in the UK, then you might consider donating them to others.

"Ask local schools, libraries or after-school science clubs whether they might like them," Dr Tonkin told BBC News's Your Voice.

"Passing items on to someone who will use them more than you is a really simple way to extend the life of something that might otherwise be thrown away."

Dr Bloomer adds: "Local astronomical societies might often take eclipse glasses in so that they have a bunch to give out to people at future events."

The Federation of Astronomical Societies has about 200 affiliated members and a searchable

list

,

external

on its website.

Repurpose them for a new hobby

With the technological abilities of modern cameras, including those on your phone, you can take good pictures of eclipses and other solar activity like sunspots, which look like dark patches on the Sun's surface.

"Cut out a square of the solar filter material [from your glasses] and mount the square over your phone's camera lens," suggests Dr Tonkin, whose Science Owl group has a challenge for children to make useful things from waste like eclipse glasses.

Dr Bloomer says "significant sunspot activity" is visible with solar filtering but that you need magnification when viewing with the naked eye.

He cautions that photographers should be wary of prolonged exposure to the Sun's UV rays.

And another thing to bear in mind - taking pictures and videos of the Sun with your phone can also damage its sensors, according to

Nasa's guidance

,

external

.

articles.title: 'Two out of four, baby' - Hunt wins 200m as she eyes historic quadruple
articles.description:
By

Emily Salley

BBC Sport journalist

Published

13 August 2026

Britain's Amy Hunt charged to 200m glory to secure her second gold medal of the European Championships - but the sprinter has her sights set on a historic quadruple in Birmingham.

The 24-year-old wants to "be iconic" and become the first athlete to win four European gold medals in the same tournament.

And after triumphing in the 100m on Monday, she added another gold to her collection with a season's best time of 22.19 seconds in the 200m final on Thursday.

Hunt reeled in rival and compatriot Asher-Smith down the back straight to cross the line first.

"Two out of four, baby!" Hunt told BBC TV.

"This is becoming a magical week and one I will remember for the rest of my life."

Hunt is set to compete in the women's and mixed 4x100m relay events later and says there will be "no celebrations and no champagne until Sunday night".

"I have got a debt to the ladies," she said.

"We have got to come out here and make sure we show them who the best sprinting nation is in Europe."

Asher-Smith was beaten to silver by just 0.01 seconds by Ireland's Rhasidat Adeleke, who set a new national record.

"It unfolded exactly how I thought it would," two-time European 200m silver medallist Nethaneel Mitchell-Blake said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I knew Dina would run a blistering bend and then say 'Amy, come and catch me'. And that's what Amy has done."

After struggling in the 200m earlier this summer, Hunt said she was ready for a "renewal of our vows" in the event.

And the Briton kept her promise with a composed performance that ended with her powering through the final 40m to beat her competitors and clinch gold.

"Amy was phenomenal. She came off that bend like a train," three-time world heptathlon champion Dame Jessica Ennis-Hill said on BBC TV.

"It was so exciting to see Dina and Amy side by side. Amy said she was going to do it - and she did."

Hunt held her arms aloft and pointed to the sky as she emulated Asher-Smith's 100m-200m European double in 2018.

"Amy has it all. The speed, the endurance, the confidence, and now the double," said former men's 1500m world champion Steve Cram.

"This is Amy's stage at the moment."

'Disappointed' Asher-Smith 'held on as hard as she could'

After getting off to a rapid start, Asher-Smith was unable to hold off Hunt and Adeleke in the final push, but in finishing third she claimed a ninth European medal - a tally only bettered by the 10 of Polish ex-sprinter Irena Szewinska.

"Dina was not handing it to Amy. She was going to make her work hard," former British 400m runner Allison Curbishley said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"Asher-Smith held on as hard as she could. Then she started to over-stride, and the hips dropped."

After finishing fifth in Monday's 100m final, Asher-Smith returned for the 200m to continue her bid to win a historic seventh gold and become the joint-most successful athlete in the history of the championships.

But there was further disappointment for the 30-year-old, who won European 200m gold in 2016 and 2018.

"I'm disappointed to have a bronze, but I think 10 years after my first one it is such an achievement to be in a place to come back year after year," Asher-Smith told BBC TV.

"It doesn't matter what's going on in my life, just come and continue to be one of the fastest women in the world. Happy to have done that today."

Before the race, there were hopes of a British one-two-three on the podium, with Asher-Smith, Hunt and Eduan holding the three fastest times in Europe this year.

However, Eduan - who beat Hunt to win her first British title in June - finished sixth.

But Hunt's second sprint gold continues Britain's dominance in the sprint events in Birmingham after Romell Glave and Jeremiah Azu secured a one-two finish in the men's 100m, while Matthew Hudson-Smith stormed to 400m victory on Wednesday.

articles.title: English makes history with European 800m gold
articles.description:
By

Andy Gray

BBC Sport NI Journalist

Published

47 minutes ago

Mark English has become the first man to win a gold medal for Ireland at the European Athletics Championships after he won the 800m in Birmingham.

English moved into first place inside the final 100 metres as he surged past Croatia's Marino Bloudek to win with a time of 1:45.26.

Ben Pattison was sixth, while there was disappointment for his Great Britain team-mate Max Burgin, who was forced to withdraw from the final after he picked up an injury in the warm-up.

But the night belonged to English, who finally won European gold after his bronze medals from 2014 in Zurich and four years ago in Munich.

The 33-year-old was the favourite for gold after he broke Olaf Beyer's 48-year European record in his semi-final at the Alexander Stadium.

And while he did not lead the final until he passed the hard-charging Bloudek turning on to the home straight, he delivered in style and fell to his knees as he crossed the line.

The gold for the Donegal runner, who is a qualified doctor, was the first medal of the Championships for Ireland before Rhasidat Adeleke claimed women's 200m silver in the following race.

Hunt surges to 200m glory to win second European gold

Published

11 minutes ago

English won his first European medal - a bronze - as a 21-year-old in 2014, and was third in Munich in 2022.

"It's just relief. I have been trying for a lifetime to get a title," English told BBC Sport.

"It was relief in 2014 when I got my first medal and relief today as well. It is just amazing.

"I have made a few changes, moved to a new coach [Justin Rinaldi] and he has been amazing. Amazing in terms of advice before races. I have to give big praise to him."

Bloudek of Croatia held on to win silver and Spain's Mohamed Attaoui claimed bronze.

Pattison, the sole British runner after the injury to Burgin, was in a strong position heading into the final 100m but fell short of a medal.

"I'm gutted. It was a great opportunity today to add to my medal collection," Pattison said.

"I gave myself too much work to do, and the legs weren't there. I'm just disappointed."

Adeleke wins silver behind Hunt

In the race after English's historic win, Ireland won their second medal of the night as Adeleke took silver in the women's 200m behind home favourite Amy Hunt.

After an injury-plagued year, Adeleke only returned to action at the Irish National Championships in the build-up to Birmingham.

The 23-year-old made a strong start and put in a late charge, and while Hunt was clear out front, Adeleke was able to pip Dina Asher-Smith on the line by just 0.01 seconds, in a time of 22.28 - a new Irish record.

It is a fourth European medal for Adeleke, who claimed a silver in the 400m in Rome two years ago.

She also won gold in the mixed 4x400m relay and a silver in the women's relay at the same Championships.

Later that year she finished fourth at the Paris Olympics in the 400m but, after an injury-hit two years since, it marks a return to form as she returned to the European podium.

With Commonwealth Games champion Kate O'Connor to come in the heptathlon, against the returning Katarina Johnson-Thompson, there are hopes the Irish medal rush has not finished yet.

articles.title: There Is $10,000 Waiting in Sydney for Any Australian Who Breaks This Record
articles.description:
Most marathon prize money goes to the international elite. The TCS Sydney Marathon has built something different underneath it.

On August 30, the Australian Marathon Championships is being contested inside the race, with what organisers describe as the richest prize purse ever offered to Australian marathon athletes.

Sitting on top of that is a $10,000 bonus for any athlete who breaks the current Australian marathon records.

The Two Numbers That Matter

The marks in question are specific and, on this course, brutally demanding.

  • Men's Australian record: 2:06:22, held by Andy Buchanan
  • Women's Australian record: 2:21:34, held by Sinead Diver

Both are legitimate world-class times. Buchanan's mark would have won the Sydney Marathon outright in most years before 2024.

Why Those Records Are Hard to Beat Here

There is an obvious problem with chasing a national record in Sydney, and it is the course.

Sydney carries roughly 313 metres of cumulative elevation gain, the most of any Abbott World Marathon Major.

There is no sustained flat section longer than a few hundred metres anywhere on the route.

National records are usually set on flat, sheltered, fast courses. Athletes travel to Berlin and Valencia for exactly that reason.

Buchanan set his 2:06:22 on a fast course, not a hilly one.

Beating it in Sydney would arguably be a more impressive run than the record itself.

That tension is what makes the bonus interesting rather than routine. It is real money placed on a genuinely difficult ask.

The Man Chasing It

Andy Buchanan is the Australian record holder and an Olympian, and 2026 marks his TCS Sydney Marathon debut.

He races on home soil, in front of a home crowd, with his own record and $10,000 on the line. That is a specific kind of pressure.

He is joined by 2025 World Athletics Championships representatives Tim Vincent and Liam Boudin, plus Sydneysider Tom Do Canto, who finished second in last year's Australian Championship.

Also in the domestic men's field is Michael Roeger, the marathon world record holder in the T46 para classification.

The Women's Championship

The Australian women's race features Tokyo Olympian Ellie Pashley and Caitlin Scott, winner of the 2025 Melbourne Marathon.

Sinead Diver's 2:21:34 is a formidable target.

To put it in perspective, that time would have finished second at the 2025 Sydney Marathon behind only Sifan Hassan and Brigid Kosgei.

In 2025, the leading Australian woman in Sydney was Leanne Pompeani, seventh overall in 2:24:47. That is roughly three minutes off the national record.

Three minutes over a marathon is a lot on a flat course.

On a course with 313 metres of climbing, it is a very large gap indeed.

Why This Prize Structure Actually Matters

It is easy to read a prize purse announcement as promotional noise. In Australian distance running it is closer to infrastructure.

Australian marathoners have historically had to travel overseas to earn meaningful prize money and to race against genuinely deep fields.

Both cost money that domestic athletes often do not have.

Putting the national championships inside a World Marathon Major solves both problems in one move.

Athletes race the best in the world without leaving the country, and they compete for money that reflects the standard.

The Development Argument

Australian Athletics has framed the 2026 field as a recruitment tool as much as a competition.

The reasoning is that young Australians watching the world's best race through their own streets are the next generation of the sport.

That is not empty rhetoric. Sydney's participation has grown from around 5,300 runners in 2022 to a record 35,000 in 2026, drawn from more than 117 countries.

Visibility of that kind changes what young athletes think is possible.

The Tactical Problem for the Australians

Here is the genuine dilemma facing every Australian in the elite field on August 30.

Do you race the national championship, or do you chase the record? They are not the same race.

Racing the championship means running tactically, covering moves from your domestic rivals, and being prepared for a slow, grinding finish.

Chasing the record means locking into an even pace regardless of what anyone else does.

On a course this hilly, even pacing by the watch is close to impossible.

Effort-based pacing is the only sane approach, which makes a time-based bonus awkward to target.

The Realistic Play

The smartest approach is probably to run with the deepest possible group for as long as it lasts.

Nineteen men in the international field have run faster than the Sydney course record of 2:06:06. A capable Australian who tucks into a fast group has a legitimate chance at a personal best.

The risk is well known.

Going with a group that is running faster than your fitness allows produces a spectacular collapse after 30 kilometres, which is exactly the failure mode explored in how to run negative splits for race day success.

That decision, made in the first 10 kilometres, will determine the Australian results more than anything else on the day.

Get The Exact Method Kenyan Runners Train With

Discover the authentic training methods of Kenyan runners and start improving your running faster than you ever thought possible.

Learn More About The Method →

Limited-time reader discount available

What to Watch on Race Day

Three things worth tracking if you are following the domestic race.

The halfway split. In 2025 the men's lead group came through in 1:03:45, and any Australian near that pace is chasing something serious.

The Oxford Street climb at 15km. This is the first place a record attempt visibly falls apart, because it is early enough to feel manageable and steep enough to cost you.

Mrs Macquarie's Chair at 38 to 40km. Whoever still has functioning quadriceps on this final climb wins the Australian title, regardless of what the clock says.

The prize structure and Australian elite athlete programme are detailed by Australian Athletics, and the full confirmed field is in the official TCS Sydney Marathon announcement.

If you are running Sydney yourself rather than watching it, the taper is now the whole game, and the evidence on doing it properly is covered in taper strategy for best marathon results.

The gun goes at 6:30am. The money is real.
